My 2c:

the_vector = c(3.3, 7.8, 10.2)
the_list = as.data.frame(t(expand.grid(lapply(as.list(the_vector), function(z) c(floor(z), ceiling(z))))))

library(microbenchmark)
# you can speed things up by passing some args to expand.grid
noams <- microbenchmark(
  the_list <- as.data.frame(t(expand.grid(lapply(as.list(the_vector), function(z) c(floor(z), ceiling(z))))))
)

noams_use_eg_better <- microbenchmark(
  the_list <- as.data.frame(t(expand.grid(lapply(as.list(the_vector), function(z) c(floor(z), ceiling(z))),
                                          stringsAsFactors=FALSE, KEEP.OUT.ATTRS=FALSE
                                          ))))
rbind(noams,noams_use_eg_better)
#    min      lq     mean   median      uq      max neval cld
# 559.203 605.864 714.6965 631.8340 738.262 1592.066   100   b
# 297.220 320.450 395.2017 334.8495 497.588  707.499   100  a

## but much more savings if you hack expand.grid to just return the list you want
## (since it constructs list internally before casting to data.frame
## for good measure, I excised all the stringsAsFactors and KEEP.OUT.ATTRS portions

eg <- function (... )
{
    nargs <- length(args <- list(...))
    if (!nargs)
        return(as.data.frame(list()))
    if (nargs == 1L && is.list(a1 <- args[[1L]]))
        nargs <- length(args <- a1)
    if (nargs == 0L)
        return(as.data.frame(list()))
    cargs <- vector("list", nargs)
    iArgs <- seq_len(nargs)
    nmc <- paste0("Var", iArgs)
    nm <- names(args)
    if (is.null(nm))
        nm <- nmc
    else if (any(ng0 <- nzchar(nm)))
        nmc[ng0] <- nm[ng0]
    names(cargs) <- nmc
    rep.fac <- 1L
    d <- sapply(args, length)
    orep <- prod(d)
    if (orep == 0L) {
        for (i in iArgs) cargs[[i]] <- args[[i]][FALSE]
    }
    else {
        for (i in iArgs) {
            x <- args[[i]]
            nx <- length(x)
            orep <- orep/nx
            x <- x[rep.int <http://rep.int>(rep.int <http://rep.int>(seq_len(nx), rep.int <http://rep.int>(rep.fac,
                nx)), orep)]
            cargs[[i]] <- x
            rep.fac <- rep.fac * nx
        }
    }
    do.call(Map, c(c, cargs))
}

hacked_eg <- microbenchmark(
  my_list <-   eg(lapply(as.list(the_vector), function(z) c(floor(z), ceiling(z))))
)
rbind(noams,noams_use_eg_better, hacked_eg)
#     min       lq     mean   median       uq      max neval cld
# 559.203 605.8640 714.6965 631.8340 738.2620 1592.066   100   c
# 297.220 320.4500 395.2017 334.8495 497.5880  707.499   100  b
# 150.168 155.7235 164.3659 159.2490 165.9545  374.378   100 a

library(testthat)
expect_equal(unname(the_list), unname(as.data.frame(my_list)))
# output matches up to names

FYI for dataheads, cool opportunity to do good things for the world with data - see below.

---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Rob Reich <re...@stanford.edu>
Date: Thu, Jul 9, 2015 at 3:39 PM
Subject: [Interesting Jobs] Project Lead, Data Science for Social Sector, at Bayes Impact, SF
To: interes...@lists.stanford.edu
Cc: er...@bayesimpact.org

Questions about this position can be directed to Eric Liu, one of the founders of the organization.

Rob

*BAYES IMPACT – TURN DATA INTO ACTION*

Bayes Impact is a technology nonprofit that uses data science to solve
pressing social challenges across the globe. We build intuitive and
powerful software applications that empower governments, nonprofits, and
individuals to make critical, data-driven decisions. We turn data into
actions that impact the lives of billions of people.

We are a small team <http://www.bayesimpact.org/about> of open-minded,
driven, egalitarian, usually sarcastic people who think there’s more to
life than ad targeting algorithms and whatever messaging app kids will use
next week. We are looking for talented, big-hearted individuals who are
hungry for hard problems that uplift people in need.

Our backers include Y Combinator, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Robert
Wood Johnson Foundation, Tableau Foundation, Linkedin For Good, and others.

*PROJECT DEVELOPMENT LEAD*

We are looking for an explorer and visionary to join our team and develop
our next big projects. Can algorithms be used to save lives by reducing
wait times for ambulance dispatch? Will better data systems improve
transparency in the criminal justice system? Is data science the key to
realizing the future of personalized health? You will identify big
questions like these and answer them with game-changing technology
solutions.

Our mission is not just to create reports and recommendations; we build
production-level software applications and deploy them in the field.
However, turning an idea into a full-fledged operational solution that
could improve the lives of millions is no small feat. If you thrive in
ambiguity and hustle by nature, this role is for you.

*THE ROLE *

We are looking for someone who can become an overnight expert in social
issues, build partnerships, engage researchers, convince funders, negotiate
roadblocks, sizing up incumbents, identify relevant technologies, devise
software solutions, and do whatever it takes to make things happen. You can
expect to:

- Research social issues and identify project opportunities where
software and data science can create transformative impact
- Develop the entire execution plan for a project; from research to
prototyping to deployment and measurement in the field
- Collaborate with our technical team to develop project concepts and
technical specifications
- Build partnerships with governments, nonprofits, and other
organizations to develop and implement solutions
- Secure funding for projects – this includes writing and
negotiating grants and contracts with foundations, governments, and other
funders
- Lead the transition from project acquisition to technical product
development by working with our technical project managers
- Devise our strategy for new project initiatives, focus areas, and
technologies

As a project development lead, you play a critical role in our
organization: Define the future of Bayes Impact’s work and create solutions
to the biggest social challenges we face today.

*FOR EXAMPLE*

A hospital is severely over capacity in their emergency department. This is
causing delays in the delivery of critical care to patients and
contributing to skyrocketing healthcare costs. Could data science be used
to identify the highest emergency department utilizers and help deploy
preventative care? What preventative care programs does the hospital run
and how can we use technology to better deploy them? What solution would we
build? Would physicians be the main users of our solution, and if so, how
would we garner adoption among them? Are there existing players and
vendors? Is our solution a significant improvement to the status quo? How
much impact will this have, and in what time frame? Is this a unique or
systemic problem; can we scale our solution to other hospitals? Are data
from the hospital’s IT systems easily accessible? Would we have to collect
new data? Who will fund this project; the hospital, a foundation, or
corporation? You will answer questions like these, and many others, in your
quest to identify and scope projects, and then own their successful
execution.

*YOU HAVE:*

- A deep passion for making the world a better place
- Technical aptitude and a strong understanding of data science and
software development. Technical experience is a plus
- Excellent writing skills. Experience writing grants and contracts is a
plus
- Strong communication and relationship management skills. You will be
representing Bayes in partnership, funding, and client conversations
- Exceptional research skills and an investigative mindset. You will
become the go-to expert in your focus areas

*APPLY*

This is a full time position located in San Francisco, CA.

If you’re interested, please send us your resume and a bit about what you
want in your work (/life/love/next meal/etc). Email us at
car...@bayesimpact.org. We’ll listen and get back to you.

_______________________________________________

Myfanwy Johnston
Ph.D Candidate, Animal Behavior
University of California at Davis

Hello wonderful Davis R Community,

Yet again, I'm consulting this great community of helpful R experts to
see if someone has any ideas on how to read in, and edit, files with
irregular combinations of letters and numbers. These data are from the
US National Historical Climatology Network. These data are in rows by
year. The first column is the station ID, subsequent rows refer to
monthly precipitation data followed by total precip with multiple
quality control notes and flags. I included the metadata as a text file
(data_format.txt) so you can see what the numbers and letters refer to.
An example of the data is attached as well.

Unfortunately when I read in the dataset with readLines I end up with a
number of issues such as uneven number of columns and letters and

Interesting problem! I took a quick crack at parsing a file and automatically looking up packages. Here’s the attempt on a script I was working on:
# Read in the file as a single character string
scripttext = paste(readLines('inst/control_test.R'), collapse="\n")

# Use a regex for all words (including _ and . characters) preceding an opening parenthesis
# There are base functions for this but I'm used to the stringi library's syntax
library(stringi)
function_names = stri_extract_all_regex(scripttext, "\\b[\\w_\\.]+(?=\\()")[[1]]

# Also, all the packages have to be loaded, I've added logic to fail gracefully

                path = sapply(function_names, function(name) {
                  path <- find(name)
                  return(ifelse(length(path) > 0, path, NA))}))

Hi all,

Hot on the heels of the last Software Carpentry, here's another!

Software Carpentry is pleased to announce that the latest in our series of workshops for women in science and engineering will be held at UC Davis on August 17-18, 2015. This workshop is aimed at those in science, engineering, medicine, or related fields who identify as women, female, or on the non-binary spectrum. Our instructors are experienced with creating safe spaces for those on the trans* spectrum, and one openly identifies as a trans woman; ensuring that we maintain an inclusive environment is a top priority for this workshop. For more information, or to register, please see the workshop website: http://camillescott.github.io/2015-08-16-ucdavis-wise/

Topics for this SWC will be :

- Automating tasks with the Unix shell
- Building programs with Python
- Version control with Git
- Managing data with SQL

Just like in speech, it's super helpful to know a second language!  Even if you are mostly an R user it's useful to pick up some Python, and everything else in this workshop complements R, as well.

As always, sign up before all the spots are taken! http://camillescott.github.io/2015-08-16-ucdavis-wise/

Do you need an official course? There are loads online through coursera or other places.

When I was first starting out I found that buying a book, reading it and following along with the examples made the most improvements in my abilities. That and lots and lots of googling for "how do I ....?". Mike Crawley's R Book is a beast, but it has loads of examples. If you're thinking of doing plotting and using ggplot2, do not buy/use the ggplot2 book that Hadley wrote, it is terribly out of date. You can build the new one he's working on here: https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2-book or Winston Chang's book is good too.

These cheatsheets from Rstudio are really handy too:
https://www.rstudio.com/resources/cheatsheets/

HTH,
Brandon

Sorry for chiming in so late - "torturing" other students in a Data Studies course :-)

Yep, I admit it - 141 is intense. Two comments -

 while based on R, the intent is computational reasoning for data analys, so those first 6 weeks
 are not just R but a lot of other aspects that we unfortunately haven't taught in other courses.

 in the "near" future, we will change STA141 & STA242 into 3 courses at both the UG and Grad. level
 that will a) make the first course less intense, b) teach more topics for data sciences
 And even better, there will be a project/capstone course in actual data analysis!!!!

Also, go to do the Data Sciences site (dsi.ucdavis.edu <http://dsi.ucdavis.edu>) and suggest different topics and formats
for materials you want to learn about.

We are doing some work in engineering soon, and one of the key premises is ongoing follow-up,
projects, user groups, etc. that allow you to internalize some of the material from courses,
workshops, etc.

 Thanks
   Duncan.
